video_title: AI Is Rewiring Retail Investing with Jim Swartwout & Jay Jacobs
gist: Two-part Risk Reversal episode: Guy Adami interviews Jim Swartwout (introduced in the auto-transcript as 'Jim Swartz'), CEO of Prosperum Fintech Holdings and a four-decade brokerage operator from Schwab, E*TRADE, Scottrade and Robinhood, on how AI bots, zero commissions and collapsed payment-for-order-flow economics are reshaping retail brokerage; then Dan Nathan interviews Jay Jacobs, BlackRock's US head of equity ETFs, on IQQQ, SOXX, tokenization, Korea's leveraged-ETF blowup and how to own the full AI value chain. The core investable thread is access: fractional shares, low-priced ETFs, private-market and prediction-market products are widening the retail funnel while index concentration forces investors to take an explicit view on the Mag 7 and semis.

themes.theme: Retail brokerage economics after zero commissions

insights.claim: Payment for order flow economics have collapsed from about a nickel per share in the late 1980s to roughly $0.0001 per share today, which Jim Swartwout argues removes PFOF as a legitimate cost objection to retail trading.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: If per-share PFOF economics are this compressed, brokerage revenue growth has to come from account growth, margin, securities lending and premium services rather than order-flow rebates — watch which brokers actually disclose the mix.
insights.quote: whenever I hear arguments about payment for order flow, payment for order flow was a nickel a share when I started. It's point zero zero zero one now. I mean, it's it's not a problem. It's never been a problem.

insights.claim: Swartwout says it is effectively impossible to compete on price in retail brokerage now that commissions are zero, so differentiation has shifted to bespoke service, experienced human brokers and embedded AI.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Expect brokerage margin pressure and consolidation among undifferentiated fintech entrants; the survivors monetize service layers, not trades.
insights.quote: it's hard to compete right now at zero commissions. You know, you have to differentiate yourself somehow.

insights.claim: Swartwout predicts the industry moves from 24/5 trading to full 24/7 equity trading as a certainty rather than a possibility, framing it purely as a timing question.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: 24/7 equities changes overnight market-making, clearing and risk-management economics — a build-out opportunity for venues and clearing infrastructure and a cost problem for brokers without overnight staffing.
insights.quote: You can trade 24/5 now at some firms. We're going to 24/7 without a doubt. It's just a matter of time.

insights.claim: Prosperum's Avant Garde broker-dealer launched its retail platform in April with equities, options and ETFs plus a partnership giving accredited investors access to private markets including SpaceX, and is planning to add futures and crypto later.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Private pre-IPO access is becoming a standard retail brokerage feature rather than a niche — a distribution channel worth tracking for secondary-market pricing of names like SpaceX.

insights.claim: Swartwout says crypto is 'in an odd place right now' and that the lack of urgency around it is why Prosperum has not rushed to add crypto trading despite planning to.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: A brokerage operator deprioritizing crypto onboarding is a soft demand signal for retail crypto volumes and exchange take rates.
insights.quote: Crypto's kind of in an odd place right now, so it hasn't been a rush.

themes.theme: AI bots as the new full-service broker

insights.claim: Prosperum's stated AI goal is to recreate 1980s full-service broker attentiveness — proactive account reviews, expiring-options alerts, roll suggestions — without a human on the line, with bots explicitly designed to be full-service brokers.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: If AI collapses the cost of advice, the durable moat in retail brokerage moves from execution price to proactive account intelligence — a threat to human RIA and call-center cost structures.
insights.quote: We want our bots to be full-service brokers, basically. And we're on our way there.

insights.claim: Avant Garde already runs a customer-facing voice bot named Alex that handles strategy conversations overnight when human brokers are off-desk, plus an internal bot that answers account-level questions.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Overnight voice AI is the cheapest way to support a 24/7 trading push — a concrete example of AI directly substituting for night-shift brokerage headcount.
insights.quote: if you really want to have fun with a voice bot and talk to someone who doesn't sound like a computer, just call our phone number that's listed there on the website after 5:00 Eastern and Alex, our our voice bot, will answer up for you.

insights.claim: Prosperum has outsourced research and analytics to a third-party AI partner, Winston AI, whose responses are surfaced inside the Avant Garde trading app alongside its own bot.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Brokers are buying rather than building AI research layers, creating a B2B market for embedded financial-research LLMs sold into brokerage front ends.

insights.claim: Prosperum offers letter-of-direction trading where a newsletter subscriber's recommended trades are executed automatically without the client placing them, and it lets third-party trading communities route orders through its APIs.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Newsletter- and community-driven auto-execution turns social sentiment into mechanical order flow, amplifying the concentration and crowding effects discussed elsewhere in the episode.

insights.claim: Swartwout argues AI tools plus fractional trading have removed the capital barrier to portfolio construction, so a $500 account can now be managed like a portfolio that historically required around $10,000.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: The addressable retail account base expands downward in balance size, which favors platforms monetizing per-account rather than per-dollar.
insights.quote: you don't have to have, you know, $10,000 to trade. You can have $500 and still build a portfolio

themes.theme: Retail flow behaviour: crowding, community, and the shift away from day trading

insights.claim: From his Robinhood years Swartwout observed that retail flow always concentrated in one or two dominant stocks at a time, with the top name holding for months before flow rotated wholesale into the next one.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Retail crowding is serial and rotational rather than diversified — a mental model for timing single-name gamma and short-squeeze setups.
insights.quote: retail tends to move in waves and they shift from one to another stock and you see one being the top stock for months and then suddenly the other one takes over.

insights.claim: Swartwout attributes current market concentration substantially to social-media-driven trading discussion and says it is visible directly in daily market volumes, while judging it risky only 'if it gets out of hand.'
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Volume concentration is a tradable tell for where social flow is parked; monitor it as a crowding gauge rather than a valuation signal.

insights.claim: Swartwout explicitly retires the 'dumb money' framing for retail, arguing that community debate before trades has made retail better informed than some professionals rather than merely more active.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Strategies premised on fading retail as uninformed flow are increasingly mispriced; the edge now sits in crowding and positioning, not information asymmetry.
insights.quote: we used to call, you know, pure retail dumb dumb money. I mean, it's not anymore. There's there's no doubt retail has as much information as anyone else, if not more in some cases.

insights.claim: Swartwout says retail behaviour has structurally shifted away from 1990s-style day trading toward weekly dollar-cost averaging into fractional shares and ETFs, which he argues mechanically props the market higher.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: A persistent passive bid from systematic retail contributions helps explain dip-buying resilience and argues against expecting retail capitulation on drawdowns.
insights.quote: back in the '90s everyone was day trading. People aren't day trading anymore.

insights.claim: Swartwout names prediction markets as the single most surprising area of client demand and openly says he does not understand why investors use them.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Prediction-market demand is running ahead of even veteran brokerage operators' expectations — a growth vector for venues and a likely regulatory flashpoint.
insights.quote: I think the one that surprised me the most is prediction markets. I don't quite understand why you would do prediction markets, but that's just my personal personal opinion.

insights.claim: Client geographic interest has rotated from European markets last year back into US markets this year, according to Swartwout, driven simply by relative US market strength.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Retail geographic allocation is momentum-following, so any sustained US underperformance would likely trigger an equally abrupt rotation out.

insights.claim: Swartwout says options are no longer treated as lottery tickets by retail and that once properly educated, customers recognize options are not inherently riskier than other trades — with Avant Garde building a 10-part on-demand webinar series from basics to spreads and straddles.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Structural growth in retail options education supports continued expansion of retail options volume, a key revenue line for brokers and market makers.
insights.quote: once customers really understand stand options, they understand that they're not any riskier than most other trades.

themes.theme: Macro read: valuations, suppressed VIX, and the midterm setup

insights.claim: Swartwout names valuation as his single biggest market concern, drawing the analogy to the 2000 and 2007-2008 reversals and warning that when valuation resets occur they are brutal.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: A brokerage CEO flagging valuation rather than liquidity as the risk supports positioning for a multiple-compression event rather than a flow-driven one.
insights.quote: valuation is the biggest concern I have with some of the companies that are out there right now.

insights.claim: Swartwout says this year's earnings have been exceptional with very few misses and small ones at that, but warns forward projected earnings must keep pace or current prices become a problem.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: The bull case is explicitly earnings-dependent — forward estimate revisions, not rates, are the variable to monitor for the top.
insights.quote: the forward projected earnings have got to keep up, or else we're going to have an issue with some of these prices.

insights.claim: With the VIX below 15 against historic single-stock volatility, Swartwout concedes the divergence is odd and inexplicable, attributing the low index vol to investor confidence that the market keeps grinding forward.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Cheap index vol against expensive single-name vol is a live dispersion trade setup, and cheap index hedges relative to realized idiosyncratic risk.
insights.quote: you have a VIX as we're sitting here today, which is south of 15, which to me is remarkable

insights.claim: Swartwout reframes index point moves as misleading, noting a 1,000-point Dow-scale move today is trivially small relative to what a 200-point move represented a decade ago.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Headline point moves systematically overstate perceived volatility to retail; percentage-based framing explains why realized index vol stays low despite dramatic headlines.
insights.quote: a 1,000-point move now is nothing compared to what like a 200-point move was 10 years ago.

insights.claim: Swartwout says client demand for portfolio hedging is elevated right now precisely because the low-volatility backdrop is hard to explain, and he expects volatility to rise into the midterm election as polls emerge.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Supports owning volatility into the midterms and selling it after — a calendar-structured vol trade with a defined catalyst.

insights.claim: Swartwout predicts the market rallies after the midterm election regardless of which side wins, because the outcome itself removes uncertainty.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: An outcome-agnostic post-election rally call implies the tradable variable is the vol crush, not directional political positioning.
insights.quote: I think post-election, regardless of the results, the market's going to rally because it'll have more certainty, more clarity.

insights.claim: Swartwout argues equities keep rising largely because rates leave investors nowhere else to earn a decent return, which is why the market did not fall over the last three months despite war and other headline risks.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: A TINA-style explanation means the equity bid is rate-sensitive at the margin; a meaningful yield backup would be the mechanism that breaks the grind higher.

themes.theme: ETF proliferation and engineering around index concentration

insights.claim: BlackRock now runs close to 1,700 ETFs globally, and Jay Jacobs says every launch must clear three filters: a genuine investment rationale, a demonstrated client need, and BlackRock's product-quality bar including market-maker support.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: The three-filter test is the stated reason BlackRock cedes leveraged and inverse product share to competitors — a structural gap for rivals like ProShares-style issuers.

insights.claim: In the first half of this year an average of six ETFs launched every business day in the US, and there are now more listed ETFs than single stocks in the United States.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: Product supply now exceeds underlying single-name supply, implying brutal fee competition and a coming shakeout of subscale funds.
insights.quote: In the first half of this year, there's been six ETFs on average launching every business day. And yes, there are more ETFs than single stocks listed in the United States now.

insights.claim: BlackRock launched IQQQ, an iShares Nasdaq 100 ETF, at 12 basis points waived to 10 basis points through July 31, 2027, deliberately priced as a low-fee compounding vehicle competing with the QQQ.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: A direct fee attack on one of the largest and most profitable ETFs in the market — watch QQQ's fee response and asset migration as the tell.
insights.quote: It is 12 basis points, way down to 10 basis points through July 31st, 2027.

insights.claim: IQQQ was deliberately launched at a low share price so an investor with as little as $25 can buy a whole share, and Jacobs notes options traders separately wanted a lower-priced Nasdaq 100 underlying for more accessible options strategies.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: Share-price engineering is now an explicit distribution lever for both first-time investors and retail options flow — a template other issuers will copy.
insights.quote: even the smallest investors who might only have $25 to invest can get a whole share of this ETF and start building that position over time

insights.claim: BlackRock split the Nasdaq 100 into QTOP (top 30 names) and QNEXT (next 70) so clients can take an explicit long or short view on Mag 7 concentration rather than accepting the index weighting.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: These two funds are a clean pair-trade instrument for the mega-cap-versus-broadening debate without single-stock risk.
insights.quote: Like it or not, you really need to think about concentration as a function of the markets that we're in today, and it's really about bringing out more tools for investors to be able to express a view on it.

insights.claim: Dan Nathan notes the top 10 names in the Nasdaq 100 — the Mag 7 plus three others — make up nearly 50% of the index weight, which is why product-level concentration control now matters more than index selection.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Buying the Nasdaq 100 is effectively a concentrated mega-cap bet; investors seeking diversification need to layer QNEXT-style or capped products on top.

insights.claim: Nathan argues SOXX is better constructed than SMH because SMH's top two holdings, Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor, are a little more than 30% of the fund, while Jacobs confirms SOXX caps single-name exposure at around 7 to 8%.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan and Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Capped versus uncapped semi ETFs are materially different trades: SMH is a leveraged Nvidia/TSMC proxy, SOXX is the diversified sector expression.

insights.claim: Jacobs argues semiconductors have graduated in three years from an interesting cyclical subsector to a foundational component of the economy, such that every investor now needs an explicit view on their semi exposure the way they would for healthcare or energy.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: Reframing semis as a core sector rather than a cyclical trade implies structurally higher baseline allocations and lower cyclical discount rates for the group.
insights.quote: semiconductors went from kind of this interesting cyclical subsector to something that is now essentially a foundational component of our economy.

insights.claim: Nathan uses the 2022 bear market as the case for index over single-name exposure: the Nasdaq fell roughly 33-34% at the lows while Nvidia, Tesla, Meta and Netflix each sold off around 70%.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Quantifies the idiosyncratic drawdown premium retail pays for single-name conviction — the core sales argument for dollar-cost-averaged index exposure.

themes.theme: Tokenization, Korea's leveraged-ETF blowup, and the AI value chain

insights.claim: Jacobs frames tokenization as having two distinct payoffs — 24/7 global access to US-based assets, and operational friction and cost reduction — positioning it as the next iteration of what ETFs already did for liquidity and access.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: The world's largest asset manager treats tokenization as an access and cost story rather than a crypto story — a signal for where institutional tokenization capital actually flows.

insights.claim: Jacobs cautions that 24/7 tokenized trading fails without first building a market-making and regulatory environment around it, because ETF market quality depends on the robust market-maker ecosystem that took years to develop.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: The bottleneck for tokenized equities is liquidity provision and regulation, not blockchain technology — favors incumbent market makers over crypto-native rails.
insights.quote: if you expand assets to trade 24/7, that's one of the first considerations is building liquidity in a market making environment and a regular regulatory environment around it uh to promote market quality.

insights.claim: Nathan reports that Korean retail investors lost more than $35 billion in the recent KOSPI correction, with people protesting outside fund management companies, after SK Hynix and Samsung grew to a little more than 50% of the index and leveraged and inverse ETFs came to dominate KOSPI-related volume.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: A live case study in what concentrated index plus levered retail products does on the way down — a template risk for US mega-cap concentration and single-stock leveraged ETFs.
insights.quote: since you had this correction over the last few weeks or so, you know, retail investors have lost more than 35 billion dollars.

insights.claim: BlackRock has deliberately never launched daily inverse or leveraged ETFs, offering delta-one country exposure like its iShares MSCI South Korea fund plus options-based income and buffer strategies instead, because levered products fail its quality and investment-thesis filters.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: The largest issuer abstaining from the fastest-growing retail product category is both a reputational stance and a ceded revenue pool worth watching if regulators tighten.
insights.quote: But today we have not brought out daily inverse or leveraged ETFs.

insights.claim: Nathan states flatly that leveraged and inverse ETFs are dangerous casino-like products for non-nimble traders and that Risk Reversal and Fast Money have never discussed using them to express a view.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Notable that the levered-product boom lacks endorsement from experienced derivatives traders — the flow is retail-driven and vulnerable to a regulatory or sentiment reversal.
insights.quote: I mean in many ways it just seems like a casino sort of product.

insights.claim: Jacobs sizes AI's economic impact at something on the order of $10-15 trillion over the next several years while stressing it is still early, and argues the hard part is pricing something this early in its evolution.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: BlackRock's house number for the AI opportunity — the anchor figure behind its active AI product push and a benchmark for judging whether current AI valuations already discount it.
insights.quote: this could be, you know, something to the order of 10, 15 trillion dollars of economic impact over the next several years.

insights.claim: Jacobs argues the market has focused too narrowly on GPUs and hyperscalers, and maps the fuller AI value chain as power infrastructure, physical data centers and their real estate, the wider semiconductor stack beyond GPUs including CPUs and memory, proprietary-data owners, frontier model developers, and finally AI-adopting application companies.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: A checklist for diversifying an AI book away from the crowded GPU/hyperscaler trade into power, real estate, data owners and AI adopters.
insights.quote: the markets have been really narrowly focused on just a couple of names and a couple of different components of the AI ecosystem.

insights.claim: BlackRock launched BAI, an actively managed AI ETF run by fundamental equities technology PM Tony Kim, on the thesis that an early, rapidly evolving theme requires active navigation rather than a static index.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: Active ETFs are the vehicle BlackRock is using to monetize theme uncertainty — track BAI's holdings as a read on institutional AI value-chain positioning.

insights.claim: Jacobs traces ETF growth to a single durable driver — access — noting single-country funds once let investors isolate Brazil or Taiwan when the only prior emerging-market proxy was buying global soft-drink manufacturers, and that the same access logic now drives thematic, Bitcoin and active ETFs.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: Access, not fees or performance, is the through-line predicting which new ETF categories gather assets — useful for screening the six-per-day launch flood.
